Kwame worked as a nurse at a busy clinic in Accra, and all week his mind kept drifting to his mother's hospital tests back in Kumasi and his brother's school fees. By Wednesday he had almost handed a patient the wrong form. So he tried something. At the start of each shift, he wrote the worries on a card, "Ma's results. Kofi's fees," and put it in his locker. "Not now," he told himself. "At seven."
At seven each evening he sat on the porch with the card and a cup of tea for half an hour. He let himself worry, made one call if needed, and wrote down one next step. Some nights he cried a little. His wife, Rania, sat with him on Thursday. By the weekend he was sleeping better, and at work his mind stayed on the patient in front of him.

qa.q: What did Kwame write on the card at the start of each shift?
qa.a: "Ma's results. Kofi's fees."

qa.q: Why did telling himself 'Not now, at seven' help Kwame at work?
qa.a: Knowing the worries had a set time and wouldn't be ignored let him put them down and focus on patients without feeling he was abandoning his family.

qa.q: What makes Kwame's 'box' healthy rather than avoidance?
qa.a: It has a door: every evening at seven he opens it, lets himself worry, makes a call if needed and writes a next step.

qa.q: How might Rania experience the half hour on the porch?
qa.a: As a chance to share his worries instead of watching him carry them silently, which may bring them closer.

grounding: A nurse in Ghana sets family worries aside during shifts and deliberately opens them for half an hour every evening.

At the government school where he taught physics, Manoj had a rule this term. From the first bell to the last, his worries about his father's surgery stayed in a box. When a thought crept in during class, he jotted "Papa - later" on a scrap and pocketed it.
Then, at 3:40, after the final bell, he sat alone in the empty staffroom for twenty minutes. He took out the scraps, let himself feel scared, called the hospital or his sister, and wrote one thing he could do that evening.
His colleague Siddharth found him there one day, eyes red. "You okay?"
"This is my worry slot," Manoj said, and laughed shakily. "If I don't give it a time, it takes all my time."
Siddharth sat down. "Can I borrow the idea? My landlord situation is eating my brain."

qa.q: What did Manoj jot on scraps during class?
qa.a: "Papa - later".

qa.q: Why does Manoj say, 'If I don't give it a time, it takes all my time'?
qa.a: Without a set slot, the worry about his father would leak into every class; knowing it had its own time let him focus.

qa.q: Why does the 3:40 worry slot work as a box with a door?
qa.a: The box keeps the worries out of class, but the daily twenty minutes opens it to feel, call and plan, so nothing gets buried.

qa.q: What might Siddharth feel on seeing Manoj's red eyes and hearing about the worry slot?
qa.a: Concern at first, then relief and curiosity, recognising a tool that could help with the landlord worry.

grounding: A teacher keeps worries about his father's surgery out of class and opens them in a fixed twenty-minute slot after school.

Dear Reena,
I know I've seemed far away lately. I want to explain, and to ask for something.
Since the restructuring at work was announced, I've been worrying about my job all day, every day, at the office and at home. I tried shoving it out of my head completely, but it just leaked out at 3 a.m.
So I'm trying something new. At work I keep it in a box: when the worry comes, I write it down and tell myself, "Tuesday and Friday." Then on Tuesday and Friday evenings, from 8 to 8:30, I open the box. I look at the list, feel however I feel, update my CV, send one email. Then I close it again.
Would you sit with me on Friday at 8? Not to fix anything. Just so I'm not opening it alone.
Love,
Joseph

qa.q: When does Joseph open the box?
qa.a: On Tuesday and Friday evenings, from 8 to 8:30.

qa.q: Why did shoving the worry out completely not work for Joseph?
qa.a: A worry with no door just leaked out at 3 a.m.; only giving it a set time let Joseph feel safe setting it aside.

qa.q: What makes Joseph's plan a healthy use of a 'box'?
qa.a: It holds the worry during work but opens on set evenings to feel it and take one action, like updating the CV or sending an email.

qa.q: How might Reena feel reading 'so I'm not opening it alone'?
qa.a: Touched and relieved to understand Joseph's distance, and glad to be invited in rather than shut out. 🤍

grounding: An adult worried about job cuts sets the worry aside at work and schedules two evenings a week to feel and act on it.

Mehak, you keep asking how I stay so calm at the dispensary. Honestly? I'm not calm. Since Nani fell in her kitchen in Nashik, and she still lives alone, I worry about her all the time. For a month I carried it behind the counter. I'd be counting tablets and suddenly picture her on the floor. Twice I had to recount a whole order.

So now I do this. When the worry shows up at work, I say to myself, "Not here, Disha. Seven o'clock." I even write it on the back of my hand sometimes. And at seven, on the bus home, I actually open it. I call Nani, I let myself feel scared, I message the neighbour aunty, I plan one thing for the weekend. Then I put it away till the next evening.

It isn't locking it up. It's giving it an appointment.

qa.q: What did Disha have to do twice at the dispensary before trying the new habit?
qa.a: Disha had to recount a whole order twice.

qa.q: Why does saying "Not here, Disha. Seven o'clock" feel possible to Disha, when simply ignoring the worry did not?
qa.a: Disha trusts that the worry will really get its turn at seven, so pausing it doesn't feel like abandoning Nani. The promise is kept every evening, which makes it believable.

qa.q: What was the turning point that let Disha focus at work again?
qa.a: The moment Disha stopped just carrying the worry all day and gave it a fixed time on the bus home, with real actions like calling Nani and the neighbour. Keeping that appointment every evening is what makes the daytime pause work.

qa.q: How might Nani experience Disha's seven o'clock routine?
qa.a: Nani likely gets a steady call every evening and knows the neighbour is in touch, so she may feel looked after rather than worried over in scattered bursts. The routine gives her something to expect.

grounding: Shows an adult who keeps a family worry out of working hours by giving it a set evening time in which that worry is felt and acts on it.

I sit next to Harsha at the textile studio in Jaipur, so I notice things. In March her landlord said he might sell the building, and she'd have to find a new room before the monsoon. For a week she was all over the place: wrong thread counts, three coffees by eleven, her phone face-up on the cutting table.

Then something changed. Every day at 5:30 she takes her notebook up to the terrace, alone, for about twenty minutes. Once I went up to hang swatches and saw her staring at the water tank, eyes wet, then writing fast. When she came down she said, "Done for today," and closed the notebook with a snap.

I don't know exactly what's in it. I asked once. She said, "Room lists, the rent, whatever's scaring me. It gets the terrace, not the looms."

Since then her samples have been perfect. She even laughs at lunch again.

Gargi

qa.q: Where does Harsha go every day at 5:30?
qa.a: She takes her notebook up to the terrace, alone, for about twenty minutes.

qa.q: What does Harsha's line "It gets the terrace, not the looms" suggest she believes?
qa.a: She seems to believe the worry deserves real attention, but only in its own place and time. Keeping that promise lets her trust herself to set it down while she works.

qa.q: What small step helped Harsha steady herself, and why does it work?
qa.a: She chose one fixed daily slot to feel the fear and write room lists, then closed the notebook. Because the worry knows it will be heard, it stops pushing into her work.

qa.a: Gargi only sees the outside: the terrace trips, wet eyes and a closed notebook. Gargi has to guess from those cues and from one short answer, so Gargi can't know for sure how Harsha feels.

grounding: An observer describes a colleague who sets aside a housing worry during work and opens it deliberately at a fixed time on the terrace each evening.
